concepts.decision: Use verified facts to decide containment, alternate-site use, restoration order, and escalation.
concepts.definition: A safety-aware assessment that establishes disruption scope, recoverability, dependencies, evidence needs, and whether the recovery strategy remains viable.
concepts.failureExample: Skipping assessment can make teams restore the wrong scope or contaminate evidence and backups.
concepts.label: DR Assessment

concepts.decision: Restore in dependency-aware order using approved sources, protected credentials, and recorded execution evidence.
concepts.definition: Controlled rebuild or recovery of prioritized services, data, identities, configurations, and dependencies from trustworthy sources.
concepts.failureExample: A service can appear online while missing data, identity services, interfaces, or required security configuration.
concepts.label: Restoration

concepts.decision: Validate functionality, dependencies, performance, monitoring, and required workflows before release to users.
concepts.definition: Technical and business checks that the restored service performs its defined functions within recovery criteria.
concepts.failureExample: A successful boot or health check alone does not prove the business service is usable.
concepts.label: Service Validation

concepts.decision: Compare recovery-point targets, record counts/checks, transactional consistency, and business reconciliation results.
concepts.definition: Evidence that recovered data is complete enough for the approved recovery point, internally consistent, authorized, and fit for intended use.
concepts.failureExample: Loading an old or inconsistent copy can silently corrupt downstream decisions and records.
concepts.label: Data Integrity

concepts.decision: Validate the controls required for the service before widening access or ending heightened monitoring.
concepts.definition: Verification that restoration re-establishes identities, authorization, encryption/key use, logging, vulnerability state, and protective monitoring.
concepts.failureExample: A fast restore that bypasses access control, keys, patches, or logging may create a second incident.
concepts.label: Security Validation

concepts.decision: Accept only after technical evidence, business workflow checks, known limitations, and risk disposition are recorded.
concepts.definition: The accountable business owner’s decision that validated recovery meets the agreed service, data, risk, and operational criteria.
concepts.failureExample: Technical completion is not business acceptance; returning users without owner acceptance can conceal unacceptable loss or limitation.
concepts.label: Service Acceptance

concepts.decision: Transition when normal capability is stable, residual risks are accepted, recovery work is documented, and rollback/contingency is understood.
concepts.definition: A controlled transition from recovery mode to normal operations, including reconciled data, stable monitoring, communications, and closure criteria.
concepts.failureExample: Premature transition can reintroduce failed dependencies, lose recovery evidence, or leave users on an unsupported temporary service.
concepts.label: Return To Normal

concepts.decision: Preserve evidence sufficient for safety, audit, reconciliation, learning, and later decision review.
concepts.definition: Time-stamped, attributable records of decisions, sources, changes, tests, results, exceptions, and acceptances made during recovery.
concepts.failureExample: A narrative without logs, test results, or approver identity cannot substantiate that recovery criteria were met.
concepts.label: Recovery Evidence

concepts.decision: Prioritize findings by service and risk impact, assign action evidence, update controlled artifacts, and retest.
concepts.definition: A controlled improvement loop that converts validated recovery observations into owned actions and retestable plan/capability changes.
concepts.failureExample: Treating lessons as a retrospective-only discussion leaves known recovery defects unresolved.
concepts.label: DR Lessons Learned

misconceptions.claim: If the application responds, restoration is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Identity, data integrity, keys, authorization, monitoring, dependencies, performance, and business workflow still require validation.

misconceptions.claim: Lessons learned belong only in the incident report.
misconceptions.correction: Recovery findings should update DR plans, architecture, controls, training, supplier commitments, and test objectives with accountable owners.

outcome: Given an activated DR event, sequence restoration, validate integrity and security, obtain service acceptance, and document residual risk and lessons.

sections.body: Assessment identifies affected facilities, systems, data, identities, networks, suppliers, people, and evidence; it also tests whether the assumed recovery strategy is still available. Restore from a trustworthy source in an order that makes dependencies and security controls usable, such as identity, network, keys, management, data, application, and monitoring as appropriate to the service. Control emergency changes and access, record deviations, and protect original evidence. A restoration step is not complete merely because a host or process starts.
keyPoints: Assessment updates the recovery decision when the event changes the assumptions.
Dependency order should include security and monitoring services, not just application tiers.
Emergency access and changes need bounded authority and later review.
sections.title: Assess damage and restore in dependency order

sections.body: Validation tests data integrity, configuration, identity and authorization, encryption and keys, logging and detection, vulnerability state, interfaces, performance, and business workflows. Technical owners confirm controls; business owners confirm that the service supports the priority function; security and risk owners accept or escalate residual risk. Return to normal only after the original service, alternate service, or new design has a documented transition plan, monitoring, communications, and rollback. Capture timing, gaps, costs, and lessons for plan and architecture changes.
keyPoints: Availability without integrity, authorization, or monitoring is not a trustworthy recovery.
Business acceptance is distinct from technical smoke testing.
Return-to-normal is another controlled change and can reintroduce the original failure.
sections.title: Validate security, business function, and return

learningJob.plainExplanation: An application response is not proof of complete restoration. Identity, keys, data integrity, authorization, monitoring, performance, dependencies, business workflow, and residual risk require validation and acceptance.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: The dependency chain with separate technical, security, and business gates shows exactly why application response precedes rather than equals accepted recovery.
